newsitem.title: INDIA: Arrest warrant spells more trouble for India's Rao.
newsitem.headline: Arrest warrant spells more trouble for India's Rao.

text.p: A legal net tightened around former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao on Friday when a judge issued a warrant for his arrest in a forgery case.
The Delhi High Court quickly suspended the warrant until a hearing next week.

But the lower court judge's order brought the former Congress party leader a step closer to becoming the first former prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges. The judge ordered Rao to appear in court on October 14.
"If I say it (the warrant) has not affected the party's image, it will be a lie," the new Congress chief, Sitaram Kesri, said after the arrest warrant was issued.
The warrant empowered authorities to arrest Rao, who served as prime minister from mid-1991 until last May and opened India to foreign investment and trade.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) charged Rao and three others on September 26 in the forgery case involving an alleged attempt in 1989 to tarnish the reputation of V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
The core allegation against Rao is that he asked Indian diplomats to attest as true what appeared to be a false documents showing a bank account in St.Kitts.
Rao's lawyers immediately won him a reprieve when the High Court suspended the warrant until a hearing next Monday.

The Press Trust of India (PTI) said Rao's lawyers cited his illnesses--diabetes and heart disease--among reasons in seeking anticipatory bail in the event of his arrest. Indian law allows an accused to seek bail to pre-empt arrest.
At Monday's hearing, the court will take up Rao's demand for legal protection against arrest in the forgery case.

Rao was denied such protection last month in a separate criminal conspiracy case which was to come up at a court hearing on October 9. The former prime minister also faces possible arrest in that 13-year-old cheating case.
Rao quit in disgrace as Congress leader last month when a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court to face charges in the $100,000 criminal cheating case.
Congress, hobbled by allegations of corruption, went down to its worst ever defeat in general elections ended in May.

The opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) said it was "a sad day" for Indian democracy. "This is what he (Rao) had planned for his opponents when he was in power and now he has come to the same pass himself," spokesman Yashwant Sinha said.

A senior Congress leader called the charges against Rao "fraudulent" and said Rao would remain head of the party in parliament. "Courts will not decide the credibility of political parties, but people will decide," B.P. Maurya said.

Rao's legal woes have fuelled tension between his party and Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left minority government, which depends on Congress to survive against the Hindu nationalist opposition in parliament.
Both the right-wing BJP and the communists have accused Deve Gowda's government of trying to shield Rao against the law.
PTI quoted Indian law minister Ramakant Khalap as saying that it was "legally right" for the government to ask federal investigators not to oppose an application by Rao in the criminal cheating case.
"We thought it wise to advise our investigating agency that we are prosecutors not persecutors," Khalap said.

In addition to Rao, the judge issued arrest warrants against three others, including two who had not yet been charged in the case. One was the son-in-law of former Saudi billionnaire Adnan Khashogi, the other an ex-minister in former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi's government.
